Chapter 4. Difference and Disability: Society’s Response to the “Other”
When you look past the intrigue and spectacle, Peter’s story really lets us see how society reacts to anyone who’s different. From the very moment he was discovered, Peter was labeled as an outsider. Not just because he grew up wild, but because he didn’t fit what people considered “normal.” He couldn’t speak, everyday tasks were a struggle, and he often seemed lost in his own thoughts. To many, his differences were both fascinating and a little unsettling.
Back in the 18th century, ideas about disability were tangled up with superstition, emerging science, and strict social expectations. Some folks looked at Peter as a blank slate—someone who could be shaped with enough education and discipline. Others saw him as broken, a sad example of how fragile the human mind can be. And these weren’t just debates in dusty books; they shaped the way Peter was treated, day in and day out.
Caretakers and officials tried all sorts of strategies to “civilize” him. They taught him how to dress, how to eat with a fork and knife, and how to follow simple instructions. Sometimes their methods were kind. Other times, not so much. The underlying belief was always the same: Peter needed to be fixed, made as similar to the other children as possible. And when he couldn’t meet those expectations, disappointment and frustration followed.
But here’s what stands out—despite all those efforts to change him, Peter stayed true to himself. Sure, he learned a few routines, picked up a handful of words, and built connections with a few people. But he never fit neatly into that “normal” box everyone hoped for. Instead, he found his own way—creating a life defined by both his challenges and his unique strengths.
Peter’s journey shined a light on how society draws invisible lines between “us” and “them.” People who don’t fit the mold get pushed to the margins—they’re pitied, or even feared. But, every now and then, moments of real empathy broke through. Some caregivers looked past Peter’s differences and saw the person inside. They laughed with him, comforted him when he was scared, and celebrated every little victory.
The way Peter was treated echoed much larger attitudes about disability and difference. In a world obsessed with fitting in, anyone who stood out was seen as a problem to fix. But Peter’s quiet resilience pushed back against those ideas. He survived. He adapted. And he managed to make connections, no matter how many obstacles he faced.
Over time, just having Peter around made people reconsider what they believed. Some realized that being different isn’t something to “fix”—it’s simply part of being human. Of course, there were others who couldn’t let go of old prejudices, unwilling to accept what they couldn’t understand.
Through it all, Peter remained a living reminder of how complex and varied human life really is. His story challenges us to look beyond the surface—and maybe, to see difference not as a flaw, but as something that can bring us together.
